awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: AF: Small: Efficient Algorithms for Optimal Transport in Geometric Settings
awd_abstract_narration:
Optimal transport (OT) is a powerful tool for comparing probability distributions and computing maps between them. Simply put, optimal transport is the minimum-cost plan to transport mass from one distribution to the other, where the cost of transporting one unit of mass between two locations is the ground distance between the two locations. OT has been studied   extensively in mathematics, engineering, physics, economics, operations research, and computer science because of their numerous applications. Despite extensive work, computing OT plans has remained a computationally challenging problem, and  there is a large gap between the theory and practice of OT algorithms. The need for fast OT algorithms is becoming even more urgent with the proliferation of machine learning and algorithmic decision making in all disciplines. The scarcity of scalable algorithms that compute high quality transport plans  has limited the applicability OT to many applications.
 
The main goal of this project is to advance the theoretical underpinnings of OT and to bridge the gap between the theory and practice of OT algorithms. By exploiting combinatorial, geometric and statistical properties of OT, leveraging new approaches for min-cost flow, and exploiting approximation and probabilistic techniques, simple and scalable algorithms will be developed for computing high quality OT plans of both discrete and continuous distributions whose supports are compact regions in Euclidean space. The emphasis will be on designing combinatorial algorithms that not only have good worst-case running time  but that have better expected running time on stochastic or semi-stochastic inputs.  The project will also explore techniques to circumvent the curse of dimensionality, which arises in the OT of high-dimensional distributions. Building on these OT algorithms, new algorithms will be developed for data analysis (e.g. clustering, training neural networks) on a family of distributions in Wasserstein space, i.e., using OT as the distance between a pair of distributions; for quality assessment of algorithms that return a probability distribution (e.g., flood-risk-analysis algorithms that return a distribution of water over a region).

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Optimal transport is a mathematical framework for comparing probability distributions and computing maps between them. Informally, it asks for the cheapest way to move mass from one distribution to another, where cost depends on distance. It is used in machine learning, statistics, data analysis, computer vision, logistics, and operations research, but computing optimal transport distances and plans at large scale remains a major algorithmic challenge. 

The goal of this project was to develop new algorithmic foundations for optimal transport, emphasizing scalable, theoretically grounded methods relevant to practice. The project advanced geometric matching, semi-discrete optimal transport, robust and partial optimal transport, scalable approximation of Wasserstein distances, Wasserstein barycenters, one-dimensional transport primitives, incremental and online matching, dynamic algorithms, and the design of parallel large-scale optimal transport algorithms with GPU-based implementations.

A central outcome was progress on semi-discrete optimal transport, where one distribution is continuous and the other is represented by finitely many points. This model arises naturally in machine learning settings where a continuous distribution must be compared or mapped to an empirical distribution, including generative modeling, distribution alignment, representation learning, and clustering. The project developed fast approximation algorithms for computing optimal transport and the best-known Monte Carlo approximation algorithm for computing an optimal transport plan in the discrete setting. It then extended these ideas to robust and partial semi-discrete optimal transport by characterizing the geometric structure of optimal solutions and developing efficient algorithms. Building on this line, the project also gave the first efficient algorithm for computing a near-optimal transport plan between two continuous probability distributions represented as two-dimensional histograms.

The project developed algorithms for p-Wasserstein distances, a broad family of optimal transport distances. It first achieved logarithmic approximation guarantees in general metric spaces and then improved these to constant-factor approximation guarantees for a broad range of Wasserstein distances. These results make optimal transport more practical for large data sets while retaining rigorous guarantees.

Another major theme was Wasserstein barycenters and robust variants. A Wasserstein barycenter is a representative distribution computed from several input distributions. The project developed the first near-linear-time approximation algorithm for computing Wasserstein barycenters under the Euclidean metric and then extended this direction to robust and partial barycenter formulations, important when data contain noise, missing data, outliers, or unmatched mass.

The project advanced one-dimensional optimal transport and robust Wasserstein computation on the line, building blocks for sliced and projected Wasserstein methods in machine learning. Although full one-dimensional optimal transport is simple after sorting, robust and partial variants are more subtle. The project developed fast algorithms for robust Wasserstein computation on the line and for computing all partial p-Wasserstein matching costs.

The project also contributed to the design of parallel large-scale optimal transport algorithms with GPU-based implementations. A major bottleneck in discrete optimal transport is storing or accessing the full pairwise cost matrix. The project developed space-efficient cost-matrix compression methods, reducing memory use while preserving enough distance information to compute high-quality approximate transport plans on much larger instances.

The project opened a new direction on incremental, dynamic, and online optimal transport and matching. In logistics, ride-sharing, and real-time assignment, requests arrive continuously and must be processed quickly. The project developed preliminary algorithms and implementation ideas for evolving-input settings, including incremental matching and robust online matching. The GPU implementation of incremental matching is motivated by the need for response rates exceeding request arrival rates; otherwise, queues build up, increasing latency and degrading solution quality. This direction raises open questions about maintaining high-quality transport plans under insertions, deletions, and online arrivals using parallel and GPU-friendly data structures.

Project results were disseminated through publications in leading venues including STOC, SODA, ESA, SoCG, NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR. The PIs also gave invited talks and workshop presentations at FSTTCS, the Symposium on Experimental Algorithms, DIMACS Rutgers, ICERM Brown, IISc, Dagstuhl, the Hausdorff Institute Bonn, NCSU Research Day, SAS, Duke, NYU, and Tel Aviv University.

The project contributed substantially to student training and workforce development. Four Ph.D. students and one M.S. student supported by the project completed their degrees. Rachita Sowle joined Virginia Commonwealth University as an assistant professor; Kaiyi Zhang joined Walmart Labs; Pouyan Shirzadian joined the Google ML Optimization group; Keegan Yao completed his Ph.D. at Duke; and Anish Mulay completed his M.S. at NCSU and had an offer to join Amazon. The project also mentored Oliver Chubet at NCSU and Arian Zamani at Duke. Students gained training in algorithms, computational geometry, approximation methods, optimal transport, dynamic and online algorithms, GPU implementation, experimentation, and research communication.

The project influenced undergraduate and graduate education. Raghvendra created and taught “Optimal Transport in Machine Learning” at NCSU and incorporated optimal transport topics into courses on algorithms, geometric computing, and optimization. Overall, the project advanced optimal transport algorithms, trained students for academic and industrial careers, and identified open questions in scalable, dynamic, online, and GPU-based computation.
